title: Ganesha and the laughing moon
hookLine: the moon laughs at Ganesha's fall, and meets the lord of obstacles
carry: the lord of obstacles humbles pride
last: VATSALYA: LOVING GOD LIKE YOUR OWN CHILD.

lines: DON'T LOOK AT THE MOON TONIGHT.
cards: Here's a strange rule some families keep on Ganesh Chaturthi. With a clay Ganesha just carried home and drums still echoing in the street, a grandmother says: whatever you do tonight, don't look at the moon.
Kids who've never heard it immediately want to look. Why not look at the moon on Ganesha's own birthday? Because, people say, Ganesha and the moon once had a very bad evening.

teach.b: The story, as it's told, goes like this. On his birthday, Ganesha has been offered modak after modak, the sweet dumplings, and he's eaten them all. Late at night, very full, he's riding home on his mouse.
A snake crosses the path. The mouse panics, Ganesha tumbles off, and his belly splits, modaks rolling everywhere.

teach.h: THE MOON LAUGHS, AND IS CURSED.
teach.b: Up in the sky, the moon, proud of his beauty, laughs. Ganesha curses the moon: whoever looks at you will be falsely accused. The moon is horrified, and the gods come to plead.
Ganesha softens. He doesn't take the curse back completely, but he narrows it to this one night, the fourth day of his month. That's why some families keep their eyes down on Chaturthi night.
In some tellings, Krishna glimpses the moon on Chaturthi and is soon accused of stealing a well-known jewel, the Syamantaka; the Bhagavata tells how he had to find the jewel to clear his name.
People say hearing that story lifts the curse if you looked by accident. Now the teaching.
Ganesha is Vighneshvara, the lord of obstacles. Hindus pray to him first, before a wedding, an exam, a new home.

teach.h: THE LORD OF OBSTACLES HUMBLES PRIDE.
teach.b: But the tradition is honest that he also sets obstacles in the way, especially in front of pride. The moon was the most beautiful thing in the sky, and it laughed.
Ganesha put one obstacle in its path, and when the moon was sorry, he softened it.
Many teachers read it this way: the bow to Ganesha before anything begins is also a lowering of pride, and the obstacle in front of you is sometimes your own pride. He clears it when you bow.

how: Hindus pray to Ganesha first, before weddings, exams and new beginnings, as the lord of obstacles; on Ganesh Chaturthi some families avoid looking at the moon, and some read or hear the Syamantaka jewel story as a remedy if they see it by accident.

he clears the way, and in stories like this one, he also sets obstacles before pride.

games.q: you're Ganesha. the moon laughed at your fall and you cursed it. now the gods are pleading for the moon. what do you do?
o: keep the curse as it is.
soften it to one night a year.
games.why: in the telling, Ganesha narrows the curse to Chaturthi night. the lord of obstacles humbled the moon's pride, then showed mercy when asked.

practice: Before beginning anything, many Hindus say a short prayer to Ganesha that ends: nirvighnam kuru me deva, Lord, keep my way free of obstacles. Say that line on a few slow breaths out, or if you don't pray, the word clear.
Then recall a recent moment when someone laughed at you, or you laughed at someone. Feel the heat of it. On a slow out-breath, bow your head a little, and set most of it down.

wordCard.voice: Ganesh Chaturthi. Ganesha's fourth day, and the night, people say, not to look at the moon, after the lord of obstacles humbled it, then softened his curse.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Marathi modaka: a sweet dumpling, often of rice flour with coconut and jaggery, Ganesha's favorite.

carryVoice: Your line: the lord of obstacles humbles pride. And softens, when asked. See you tomorrow.
